components.note: 扌 (hand) — 摆 describes placing or swinging something with the hand.
罢 (bà) gives a sound distantly related to bǎi, having drifted apart over time.
⺼ (flesh, body) — 脱 relates to taking something off the body.
兑 (duì) gives a sound close to tuō, sharing a related initial.

example.hanzi: 他终于摆脱了那份压力很大的工作。
example.pinyin: Tā zhōngyú bǎituō le nà fèn yālì hěn dà de gōngzuò.
example.english: He finally freed himself from that very stressful job.
example.fact: 摆 (扌 "hand" + phonetic 罢) means "to swing, to place," and 脱 (⺼ "flesh, body" + phonetic 兑) literally means "to take something off the body," like shedding clothing — combined, 摆脱 pictures physically shaking something off, extended metaphorically to breaking free from a burden or bad situation.

components.note: 力 (strength) — 助 relates to helping, lending one's strength
且 (qiě) gives a loose sound connection to 助's reading zhù
手 is a simple picture of an open hand with the fingers spread out.

example.hanzi: 她是医生的助手,负责整理病历。
example.pinyin: Tā shì yīshēng de zhùshǒu, fùzé zhěnglǐ bìnglì.
example.english: She is the doctor's assistant, responsible for organizing medical records.
example.fact: 助手 combines 助 ("to help," built from 力 "strength") with 手 ("hand") into a nearly literal "helping hand" — the same image English reaches for with its own idiom "right-hand man."

components.note: 未 depicts a tree with young, unripe branches.
鬼 depicts a ghost or spirit with a strange, masked head — paired with the tree, it evokes something hidden deep in the woods, giving 魅 its meaning 'demon, enchanting.'
力 depicts the blade of a plow — since plowing fields took great physical effort, the shape came to represent strength or power.

example.hanzi: 这位演员的舞台魅力吸引了很多观众。
example.pinyin: Zhè wèi yǎnyuán de wǔtái mèilì xīyǐn le hěn duō guānzhòng.
example.english: This actor's stage charisma attracted many audience members.
example.fact: 魅 pictures a 鬼 ("ghost, spirit") lurking among 未 (young tree branches) and originally meant "demon, enchanting spirit" — so 魅力, built on that character, frames charisma as an almost supernatural, bewitching pull rather than ordinary attractiveness.

components.note: 马 (horse) — 验 originally related to examining or testing horses, later extended to 'to test, examine, verify'
佥 (qiān) gives a loose sound connection to 验's reading yàn

example.hanzi: 学生们在实验室做化学实验。
example.pinyin: Xuéshengmen zài shíyànshì zuò huàxué shíyàn.
example.english: The students are doing a chemistry experiment in the lab.
example.fact: 验 (马 "horse" + phonetic 佥) originally meant examining or testing a horse before a purchase or a long journey — its sense broadened over the centuries from that literal check-up into the general "to test, to verify" that it carries in 实验 today.

components.note: 讠 (speech) — 误 began as a mistake in speech, later broadening to 'error' in general.
吴 (wú) gives a sound close to wù, with the tone shifted.
人 (people) over 云 (clouds/say) — a picture of people gathering and speaking together, related to 会's meanings 'to meet' and 'to know how to.'

example.hanzi: 对不起,这只是一个误会。
example.pinyin: Duìbuqǐ, zhè zhǐshì yí gè wùhuì.
example.english: Sorry, this is just a misunderstanding.
example.fact: 误 (讠 "speech" + phonetic 吴) originally named an error made specifically in speaking, only later broadening to cover any kind of mistake — the sense it carries when paired with 会 ("to understand") in 误会.

components.note: 户 (a door) — the panel of a door.
口 (an opening) — the door swinging open, together giving 启 its meaning 'to open, to begin.'
力 (strength/force) — 动 relates to movement produced by exertion or force.

example.hanzi: 请按这个按钮启动电脑。
example.pinyin: Qǐng àn zhège ànniǔ qǐdòng diànnǎo.
example.english: Please press this button to start the computer.
example.fact: 启 pictures a door (户) swinging open (口) — 启动 extends that literal image of "opening up" into the abstract sense of setting a machine, process, or plan into motion.

components.note: 心 (heart) — 恋 describes a heart drawn to and longing for someone or something.
亦 (yì) is only distantly related in sound to liàn — the connection has drifted apart to the point of being barely recognizable.
冖 (a roof/house) — the home being welcomed into.
友 (a friend) — brought close into one's home; the traditional form 愛 also includes 心 ('heart') in the middle — the source of 爱's meaning 'to love.'

example.hanzi: 他们谈恋爱三年了,准备结婚。
example.pinyin: Tāmen tán liàn'ài sān nián le, zhǔnbèi jiéhūn.
example.english: They've been dating for three years and are getting ready to get married.
example.fact: 恋爱 is almost always paired with the verb 谈 ("to talk, to carry on") in the fixed phrase 谈恋爱, literally "to converse a romance" — a reminder that 恋爱 behaves more like a noun object than a stand-alone verb in everyday speech.

components.note: 八 (to divide/split) — represents something being separated into smaller parts.
亅 (a hook/line) — cutting a small piece off, an image tied to the meaning 'small, tiny.'
日 (sun/day) — relates to 时's meaning of 'time, season'; the phonetic part of the character was later replaced by 寸 in the simplified form
亻 (person) — relates to 候's meaning 'to wait, time,' as if a person watching and waiting.
矦 (hóu) gives a sound hint — 候 is pronounced hòu, sharing the same rhyme with a different tone.

example.hanzi: 小时候,我最喜欢在河边玩耍。
example.pinyin: Xiǎo shíhou, wǒ zuì xǐhuan zài hébiān wánshuǎ.
example.english: When I was little, I loved playing by the river.
example.fact: 小时候 tucks 时候 ("time, moment") behind 小 ("small, young") to mean literally "the small-time," i.e. one's early years — it works as a fixed time expression that typically opens a sentence, much like English "back then" or "as a kid."

components.note: 讠 (speech) — 话 relates to speaking and words.
舌 (tongue) — the organ used for speaking, reinforcing 话's meaning of 'speech' or 'words.'
页 (head/page) — 题 relates to the forehead or the topmost part, extending to the 'title' or 'topic' placed at the top.
是 (shì) gives a hint of the sound — 题 is pronounced tí, a connection that has shifted over time.

example.hanzi: 这个话题我们已经讨论过很多次了。
example.pinyin: Zhège huàtí wǒmen yǐjīng tǎolùn guò hěn duō cì le.
example.english: We've already discussed this topic many times.
example.fact: 话题 combines 话 ("speech, words") with 题, itself built from 页 ("head") for the "heading" placed at the top of a piece of writing — so 话题 pictures a conversation's own heading, the subject printed at the top of what's being said.

components.note: 土 (earth) — 场 relates to a flat open area of ground, such as a field or venue.
昜 (yáng) gives a hint of the sound — 场 is pronounced chǎng, a connection that has drifted significantly over time.

example.hanzi: 这种新产品在市场上很受欢迎。
example.pinyin: Zhè zhǒng xīn chǎnpǐn zài shìchǎng shàng hěn shòu huānyíng.
example.english: This new product is very popular in the market.
example.fact: 场 (土 "earth" + phonetic 昜) originally named any flattened open ground used for a specific activity, like a threshing floor or drill ground — 市场 narrows that general "activity ground" down to the ground specifically used for buying and selling.

components.note: 辶 (to walk) — 迷 originally described losing one's way while walking, extending to 'confused, obsessed.'
米 (mǐ) gives a sound distantly related to mí, having drifted apart over time.
A simple line drawing of a person's legs seen from the side, used to depict a human being.

example.hanzi: 桂林的风景非常迷人。
example.pinyin: Guìlín de fēngjǐng fēicháng mírén.
example.english: Guilin's scenery is extremely enchanting.
example.fact: 迷 (辶 "to walk" + phonetic 米) originally described losing one's way while walking — 迷人 literally means "person-losing," something so captivating it makes you lose your bearings, the same root behind 迷路 ("to get lost") and 迷恋 ("to be infatuated with").

components.note: 力 (strength) — 加 pictures adding one's effort to a cause.
口 (mouth, words) — combining strength with words of support gave 加 its meaning 'to add' or 'to increase.'
州 depicts small dots of land, like islands, surrounded by the curving lines of a river (川) — the origin of its meaning 'state, region.'

example.hanzi: 我的表姐住在加州的洛杉矶。
example.pinyin: Wǒ de biǎojiě zhù zài Jiāzhōu de Luòshānjī.
example.english: My cousin lives in Los Angeles, California.
example.fact: 加州 shortens the full transliteration 加利福尼亚州 down to just its first and last syllables — 加 (borrowed purely for its sound) plus 州 ("state, province") — the same clipping pattern behind other US state nicknames, like 德州 for Texas (德克萨斯州).

components.note: 廴 (to move forward, extend) — 建 relates to constructing or setting something up over an extended process.
聿 (yù) gives a hint of the sound — 建 is pronounced jiàn, a connection that has shifted significantly over time.
⺮ (bamboo) recalls bamboo poles used in early construction.
巩 (strong, firm) reinforces the idea of a sturdy structure, giving 筑 its meaning 'to build.'

example.hanzi: 这座建筑有两百年的历史了。
example.pinyin: Zhè zuò jiànzhù yǒu liǎng bǎi nián de lìshǐ le.
example.english: This building has a two-hundred-year history.
example.fact: 筑 pairs the bamboo radical ⺮ with 巩 ("firm, secure") — early construction work often relied on bamboo scaffolding and poles, so the character still carries a trace of that original building material even though 建筑 today covers structures made of anything.

components.note: 扌 (hand) — 举 relates to lifting or raising something with the hand
舉 (jǔ) is the traditional character's own form, giving the sound directly, an exact match
彳 depicts a step with the left foot; together with 亍 (a step with the right foot), 行 shows a person walking or moving.
亍 depicts a step with the right foot, complementing 彳 to form the idea of walking or travel.

example.hanzi: 婚礼将在下周六举行。
example.pinyin: Hūnlǐ jiāng zài xià zhōu liù jǔxíng.
example.english: The wedding will be held next Saturday.
example.fact: 举行 is reserved for formal, scheduled events — ceremonies, meetings, competitions — and sounds odd applied to a casual get-together, where Chinese instead reaches for simpler verbs like 开 ("to hold/start [a meeting]").

components.note: 扌 (hand) — 损 relates to damage or loss caused by an action.
员 (yuán) reflects the character's historical phonetic root, though the modern reading sǔn has diverged.
丿 (something falling) — an object slipping away.
夫 (a hand/person) — the object slipping out of a hand, giving 失 its meaning 'to lose.'

example.hanzi: 这场火灾造成了巨大的损失。
example.pinyin: Zhè chǎng huǒzāi zàochéng le jùdà de sǔnshī.
example.english: This fire caused enormous losses.
example.fact: 损失 works as both a noun ("a loss") and a verb ("to lose, to suffer damage") without changing form at all — a common trait of two-character Chinese compounds that English usually has to render with two separate words.

components.note: 十 — traditionally read as a great man standing tall.
一 (the two horizontal strokes) — heaven above and earth below, which the king bridges, giving 王 its meaning 'king, monarch.'
A simple drawing of a swaddled baby — arms reaching out, legs bundled together in a wrap.

example.hanzi: 那个王子最后娶了灰姑娘。
example.pinyin: Nàge wángzǐ zuìhòu qǔ le Huīgūniang.
example.english: In the end, the prince married Cinderella.
example.fact: 王子 builds directly on its two parts — 王 ("king") plus 子 ("son") — literally "king's son," one of the more transparent titles in the royal vocabulary, alongside 公主 ("princess").

components.note: 辶 (to walk) — 退 relates to moving backward or away
艮 (gèn) gives a sound distantly related to 退's reading tuì, having drifted apart over time

example.hanzi: 消防员让围观的人都退后一点。
example.pinyin: Xiāofángyuán ràng wéiguān de rén dōu tuìhòu yìdiǎn.
example.english: The firefighter told the onlookers to all step back a little.
example.fact: 退 already means "to retreat, to move backward" on its own (辶 "to walk" + phonetic 艮), and 后 means "behind, back" — 退后 reinforces the same backward direction twice, the same near-synonym doubling strategy behind words like 喜欢 and 应该.

components.note: A picture of a nose; because people in ancient China would point to their own nose when referring to themselves, the character came to mean 'self.'
豕 (boar) — 豪 originally described a fierce, bristling boar-like porcupine, extending to 'heroic, grand.'
高 (gāo) shares the rhyme -ao with háo, though the initial has drifted from g- to h- over time.

example.hanzi: 父母为孩子的成绩感到很自豪。
example.pinyin: Fùmǔ wèi háizi de chéngjì gǎndào hěn zìháo.
example.english: The parents feel very proud of their child's achievements.
example.fact: 豪 depicts a bristling wild boar (豕) with the phonetic 高 layered above — its older sense of a fierce, formidable creature broadened into "heroic, grand," the same bold flavor 自豪 keeps: not mere satisfaction, but a robust pride in one's own accomplishment.

components.note: Flesh — the belly is part of the body.
Gives the sound tǔ, related to dù but drifted apart over time.
A simple drawing of a swaddled baby — arms reaching out, legs bundled together in a wrap.

example.hanzi: 我肚子饿了,想去吃饭。
example.pinyin: Wǒ dùzi è le, xiǎng qù chīfàn.
example.english: My stomach is growling, I want to go eat.
example.fact: 肚子 is the everyday, colloquial word for the stomach or belly — the more formal, technical word for the internal organ is 胃 (wèi), reserved mainly for medical contexts.

meanings: to expel (a member of an organization)

components.note: 廾 (two hands) — depicts hands at work.
一 represents the latch or bar of a door; hands lifting it away gave 开 its meaning 'to open, to start.'
阝 (a mound/settlement) — represents a city or town.
余 (surplus, remainder) — the leftover waste a city produces, which must be cleared away, giving 除 its meaning 'to remove, eliminate.'

example.hanzi: 他因为旷工太多被公司开除了。
example.pinyin: Tā yīnwèi kuànggōng tài duō bèi gōngsī kāichú le.
example.english: He was fired by the company for missing too much work.
example.fact: 开除 carries a formal, disciplinary tone — used for expelling a student or firing an employee specifically for wrongdoing — distinct from the more neutral 辞退 or 解雇 ("to lay off"), which don't necessarily imply punishment.

meanings: (as a correlative conjunction) not only (..., but also ...)

components.note: The oracle-bone form has been interpreted as a bird flying up toward the sky; the meaning later shifted entirely to represent negation, 'not.'
亻 (person) — 仅 relates to a person or amount limited to just this much, giving its meaning 'only, merely'

example.hanzi: 她不仅会说英语,还会说法语。
example.pinyin: Tā bùjǐn huì shuō Yīngyǔ, hái huì shuō Fǎyǔ.
example.english: She can not only speak English, but also French.
example.fact: 不仅 almost always sets up a paired construction with 还 or 而且 ("but also") later in the sentence — the same "not only...but also" template English uses, making it one of the more directly transferable conjunctions for English speakers.

components.note: 大 (a person, arms outstretched) — represents a human being.
一 (a line, here representing the sky) — drawn above a person, showing what is above them: the heavens, hence 'sky, day.'

example.hanzi: 夏天的时候,这里非常热。
example.pinyin: Xiàtiān de shíhou, zhèlǐ fēicháng rè.
example.english: In the summer, it's extremely hot here.
example.fact: All four Mandarin season words follow the same "[season] + 天" pattern — 春天, 夏天, 秋天, 冬天 — with 天 (literally "sky, day") functioning as a generic time-of-year suffix rather than meaning a literal single day.

components.note: 饣 (food) — 饼 names a type of food, a flat cake.
并 (bìng) gives a sound close to bǐng, sharing the same rhyme with a different tone.
A pictograph of an ancient forked weapon, such as a club or shield-tipped spear — the tool image later extended to 干's meanings 'to do, to work' and, in another reading, 'dry.'

example.hanzi: 妈妈烤了一些巧克力饼干。
example.pinyin: Māma kǎo le yìxiē qiǎokèlì bǐnggān.
example.english: Mom baked some chocolate cookies.
example.fact: 饼 names any flat, round cake-like food — the same root appears in 月饼 ("mooncake") and 馅饼 ("a filled pastry") — while 干, read here as gān rather than its more common reading gàn ("to do"), keeps its older sense "dry," describing the biscuit's crisp texture.

components.note: 丁 (a stylized handle/hook shape in the ancient form) — part of the character's original picture, now mostly opaque in the modern form
口 (kǒu, mouth) gives a sound related to 可's pronunciation kě, and may connect to 可's sense of approval spoken aloud
夭 (a person leaning back) — the pose of someone laughing.
⺮ (bamboo-like strokes) — suggesting a wide grin, giving 笑 its meaning 'to laugh, smile.'

example.hanzi: 他的借口听起来很可笑。
example.pinyin: Tā de jièkǒu tīng qǐlai hěn kěxiào.
example.english: His excuse sounds very ridiculous.
example.fact: 可笑 leans toward the mocking end of "funny," closer to "ridiculous, laughable," while its near-twin 好笑 stays neutral or even affectionate, closer to plain "funny" — a distinction worth knowing before calling something 可笑 to someone's face.

components.note: 灬 (fire) — 热 relates directly to heat
执 (zhí) gives a loose sound connection to 热's reading rè
忄 (heart) — 情 relates to feelings and emotions.
青 (qīng) gives the sound — 情 is pronounced qíng, a close match differing only in tone.

example.hanzi: 服务员对客人非常热情。
example.pinyin: Fúwùyuán duì kèrén fēicháng rèqíng.
example.english: The waiter is extremely warm and friendly toward guests.
example.fact: 热情 covers ground English splits into several separate words — "warmth," "enthusiasm," "hospitality," "passion" — all folded into one word equally at home describing a friendly host, an eager volunteer, or a passionate romance.

components.note: 亻 (person) plus 乍 (suddenly/for the first time) — together suggesting a person making or doing something for the first time.
讠 (speech) — the act of speaking.
正 (straight, correct) — speaking the straight, correct truth, giving 证 its meaning 'to prove, certify; evidence.'

example.hanzi: 他愿意在法庭上为朋友作证。
example.pinyin: Tā yuànyì zài fǎtíng shàng wèi péngyou zuòzhèng.
example.english: He is willing to testify in court for his friend.
example.fact: 证 (讠 "speech" + 正 "straight, correct") literally means speaking the straight truth — 作证, "to make/do 证," turns that noun for "proof, evidence" into the everyday verb "to testify," the same 作 + [noun] pattern that forms 作案 ("to commit a crime").

components.note: 女 (woman) — represents a mother.
子 (child/son) — a mother together with her child was seen as an image of goodness, giving 好 its meaning 'good.'
夭 (a person leaning back) — the pose of someone laughing.
⺮ (bamboo-like strokes) — suggesting a wide grin, giving 笑 its meaning 'to laugh, smile.'

example.hanzi: 这个笑话真好笑!
example.pinyin: Zhège xiàohua zhēn hǎoxiào!
example.english: This joke is really funny!
example.fact: 好笑 is built the same way as 好吃 ("delicious," literally "good to eat") and 好看 ("good-looking," literally "good to look at") — 好 + [verb] forms an adjective meaning "good to [verb]," so 好笑 literally reads "good to laugh at."

components.note: 讠 (speech radical) — shows 说 relates to talking or language
兑 (duì) is the phonetic component; historically 说 was also pronounced closer to 兑's sound before shifting to shuō
氵 (water/stream) — water naturally follows a fixed course, an image linked to the idea of 'law' or 'method.'
去 (to go/a course) — the path a stream follows suggested a regulated, consistent way of doing things, hence 'law, method.'

example.hanzi: 关于这件事,大家有不同的说法。
example.pinyin: Guānyú zhè jiàn shì, dàjiā yǒu bùtóng de shuōfa.
example.english: Regarding this matter, everyone has a different version of events.
example.fact: CEDICT lists two distinct readings for the same two characters: the everyday shuō·fa (法 toneless) means "a way of putting things, a statement or version," while the fully-toned shuō fǎ is a much rarer Buddhist term meaning "to expound the Dharma" (讲经说法) — an easy trap for automated pinyin lookups, since only the tone on 法 tells the two apart.

components.note: 廾 (two hands) — depicts hands at work.
一 represents the latch or bar of a door; hands lifting it away gave 开 its meaning 'to open, to start.'
口 is a simple picture of an open mouth.

example.hanzi: 他想借钱,却不知道怎么开口。
example.pinyin: Tā xiǎng jiè qián, què bù zhīdào zěnme kāikǒu.
example.english: He wants to borrow money, but doesn't know how to bring it up.
example.fact: 开口 extends past its literal sense "to open one's mouth" into "to broach a difficult or awkward topic," often paired with 难 to form 难以开口 ("hard to bring oneself to say") — capturing the hesitation before saying something uncomfortable.

components.note: 囗 (a boundary/enclosure) surrounding 玉 (jade, treasure) — a country pictured as protected, valuable territory.
阝 (a mound/place) — relates to 际's meaning 'border, between,' an edge or boundary marker.
示 (shì) served as the phonetic base; its pronunciation has since drifted well away from jì.

example.hanzi: 这家公司正在拓展国际市场。
example.pinyin: Zhè jiā gōngsī zhèngzài tuòzhǎn guójì shìchǎng.
example.english: This company is expanding into international markets.
example.fact: 国际 functions only as an attributive modifier before a noun (国际市场, 国际关系) and never stands alone as "internationally" — for that adverbial sense Chinese instead uses 在国际上, a distinction easy to miss since English "international" can sit more loosely in a sentence.

components.note: 义 (yì) gives a sound close to yí, differing only in tone.
弋 (an awl or tool) — one of the craftsman's instruments.
工 (a measuring square) — a tool for making things to a fixed pattern, giving 式 its meaning 'style, form, type.'

example.hanzi: 学校为新生举行了开学仪式。
example.pinyin: Xuéxiào wèi xīnshēng jǔxíng le kāixué yíshì.
example.english: The school held an opening ceremony for the new students.
example.fact: 式 (弋 "tool" + 工 "measuring square") originally meant a model or standard for making things to a fixed pattern — 仪式 extends that same "set pattern" from craftsmanship to the fixed sequence of actions and words expected on a formal occasion.

components.note: 扌 (hand) — 投 relates to throwing something with the hand
殳 (shū) gives a loose sound connection to 投's reading tóu
入 depicts a simple wedge or arrow shape pointing inward, showing the direction of entering.

example.hanzi: 公司投入了大量资金开发新产品。
example.pinyin: Gōngsī tóurù le dàliàng zījīn kāifā xīn chǎnpǐn.
example.english: The company invested a large amount of capital to develop new products.
example.fact: 投入 stretches from the literal "to throw into" (投 "to throw" + 入 "to enter") all the way to the abstract "to invest [money, effort]" and even the adjective "absorbed, engrossed" (他工作很投入, "he's very absorbed in his work") — the same image of throwing oneself in covers financial, emotional, and mental commitment alike.

components.note: 灬 (fire) — 熟 describes food that has been cooked thoroughly over fire.
孰 (shú) gives the sound — an exact match with 熟's reading shú.

example.hanzi: 这些苹果还没有完全成熟。
example.pinyin: Zhèxiē píngguǒ hái méiyǒu wánquán chéngshú.
example.english: These apples aren't completely ripe yet.
example.fact: 熟 (灬 "fire" + phonetic 孰, an exact sound match) originally described food fully cooked over a flame — 成熟 extends that same "fully done, ready" image from cooked food to ripened fruit and, metaphorically, to a person's emotional or intellectual maturity.

components.note: 讠 (speech) — 谋 relates to discussing and forming a plan.
某 (mǒu) gives the sound — an exact match with 谋.
乂 depicts crossed strokes suggesting a cutting action.
木 (wood) here represents a wooden stake — giving 杀 its meaning 'to kill.'
木 (wood) — 案 originally referred to a wooden table or desk
安 (ān) gives a sound close to 案's reading àn, differing only in tone

example.hanzi: 警方正在调查这起谋杀案。
example.pinyin: Jǐngfāng zhèngzài diàochá zhè qǐ móushā'àn.
example.english: The police are investigating this murder case.
example.fact: 案 (木 "wood" + phonetic 安) originally named a wooden table or desk — the "case" sense in 谋杀案 grew out of documents and evidence being laid out on that desk for a judge to review, the same table-to-case extension behind the English phrase "the bench."

components.note: 氵 (water) — 混 originally described muddy, mixed water.
昆 (kūn) gives a sound distantly related to hùn, having drifted apart over time.

example.hanzi: 交通事故导致了严重的交通混乱。
example.pinyin: Jiāotōng shìgù dǎozhì le yánzhòng de jiāotōng hùnluàn.
example.english: The traffic accident caused serious traffic chaos.
example.fact: 混 (氵 "water" + phonetic 昆) originally described muddy water where clean and dirty had mixed together indistinguishably — 混乱 keeps that same core image of things jumbled together without order, whether it's liquids, traffic, or a chaotic situation.

components.note: 心 was originally a pictograph of the physical shape of a human heart, and came to represent the mind, feelings, and intention as well.

example.hanzi: 我对这次考试很有信心。
example.pinyin: Wǒ duì zhè cì kǎoshì hěn yǒu xìnxīn.
example.english: I'm very confident about this exam.
example.fact: 信心 almost always appears with 有 or 没有 (有信心 "to have confidence," 没信心 "to lack confidence") rather than as the subject of its own sentence — Chinese grammatically treats confidence as something you hold, not simply a state you are.

example.hanzi: 他一直把我当成最好的朋友。
example.pinyin: Tā yìzhí bǎ wǒ dàngchéng zuì hǎo de péngyou.
example.english: He has always treated me as his best friend.
example.fact: 当成 almost always shows up inside a 把 construction (把 A 当成 B, "to treat A as B"), with the object A fronted before the verb — a word-order pattern with no direct equivalent in English's ordinary subject-verb-object structure.

components.note: 耳 (ear) — 联 originally meant 'connected, linked,' perhaps through the image of joined loops.
关 (guān) served as the phonetic base; its pronunciation has since drifted well away from lián.
纟 (thread) — 络 relates to threads woven together into a net or web.
各 (gè) gives a sound distantly related to luò, having drifted apart over time.

example.hanzi: 请保持联络,有消息随时通知我。
example.pinyin: Qǐng bǎochí liánluò, yǒu xiāoxi suíshí tōngzhī wǒ.
example.english: Please stay in touch, let me know as soon as there's news.
example.fact: 络 (纟 "thread" + phonetic 各) pictures threads woven together into a net — 联络, pairing it with 联 ("linked, connected"), treats staying in contact as literally keeping a web of threads intact between people, much like English's own "network."

components.note: Sickness — cancer is a disease.
Gives the sound yán, related to ái but drifted apart over time.
疒 (sickness) — 症 names a symptom or disease.
正 (zhèng) is an exact match for the sound of 症.

example.hanzi: 早期发现癌症可以提高治愈的机会。
example.pinyin: Zǎoqī fāxiàn áizhèng kěyǐ tígāo zhìyù de jīhuì.
example.english: Discovering cancer early can improve the chances of a cure.
example.fact: 癌 is pronounced ái in Mandarin rather than the "regular" phonetic reading yán (matching its component 嵒) — several sources attribute this deliberate divergence to hospitals wanting to avoid dangerous mix-ups between 癌症 ("cancer") and the similarly-pronounced 炎症 ("inflammation") when spoken aloud.

components.note: 寸 here depicts a hand.
良 pictures a goblet — together, a hand holding a ceremonial wine goblet, the image behind 爵's original meaning 'noble rank.'

example.hanzi: 他被英国女王封为爵士。
example.pinyin: Tā bèi Yīngguó nǚwáng fēng wéi juéshì.
example.english: He was knighted by the Queen of England.
example.fact: 爵士 does double duty as two unrelated words sharing the same two characters: the older sense "knight, Sir" (a hand 寸 holding the ceremonial wine goblet 爵, the ancient symbol of noble rank) and the newer sense "jazz," a straightforward phonetic loan from English with no connection to the original meaning.

components.note: 毛 (fur, hair) — 表 originally pictured a fur garment worn on the outside.
衣 (clothing) — an outer fur wrap gave 表 its meaning of 'outer' or 'surface,' and later, 'to express' (showing something on the surface).
日 (sun) — combined with 月 (moon), 明 shows the light of both sun and moon, giving the meaning 'bright' or 'clear.'
月 (moon) — together with 日 (sun), the two brightest things in the sky represent brightness and clarity.

example.hanzi: 研究结果表明,运动对健康很有帮助。
example.pinyin: Yánjiū jiéguǒ biǎomíng, yùndòng duì jiànkāng hěn yǒu bāngzhù.
example.english: The research results indicate that exercise is very helpful for health.
example.fact: 表明 is a workhorse of formal and academic writing — introducing evidence, data, or a conclusion ("研究表明...", "the research indicates...") — and sounds noticeably stiff in casual conversation, where speakers reach for the plainer 说明 or just 说 instead.

components.note: A simplified pictograph of a bird's wings spread in flight — the source of 飞's meaning 'to fly.'
彳 depicts a step with the left foot; together with 亍 (a step with the right foot), 行 shows a person walking or moving.
亍 depicts a step with the right foot, complementing 彳 to form the idea of walking or travel.

example.hanzi: 这架飞机的飞行时间大约十个小时。
example.pinyin: Zhè jià fēijī de fēixíng shíjiān dàyuē shí gè xiǎoshí.
example.english: This plane's flight time is about ten hours.
example.fact: 飞行 is reserved for controlled, mechanical flight — airplanes, pilots, aviation — while a bird or insect's more ordinary fluttering about is just 飞 alone; the added 行 ("to travel, to move along") frames 飞行 specifically as sustained, directional travel through the air.

components.note: 耂 (a person bent with age, with long hair) — depicts an elderly figure.
匕 (here representing a cane or walking stick) — combined with the bent figure above, 老 pictures an old person leaning on a cane.
八 here depicts something splitting apart or being divided.
厶 is an old form meaning 'private' or 'one's own' — 公 shows dividing up private property to share it fairly, giving rise to the meaning 'public' or 'fair.'

example.hanzi: 我老公每天都做饭。
example.pinyin: Wǒ lǎogōng měitiān dōu zuò fàn.
example.english: My husband cooks every day.
example.fact: 老公 is casual, spoken-register Mandarin — the neutral, written-register word for "husband" is 丈夫 — so using 老公 in a formal document would feel about as out of place as calling your own spouse "hubby" in a business letter.

components.note: 大 (a person, arms outstretched) — represents a human being.
一 (a line, here representing the sky) — drawn above a person, showing what is above them: the heavens, hence 'sky, day.'
才 depicts a young sprout just breaking through the soil — new growth came to represent budding talent or ability.

example.hanzi: 莫扎特是音乐天才。
example.pinyin: Mòzhātè shì yīnyuè tiāncái.
example.english: Mozart was a musical genius.
example.fact: 天才 literally means "heaven-born talent" (天 "heaven" + 才, a character depicting a sprout just breaking through the soil) — framing genius as an innate gift from birth, in contrast to 人才 ("talented person," 人 "human"), which describes ability built through training and effort.

components.note: 工 depicts a carpenter's square or workman's tool — a simple shape that came to represent work and labor.
八 (two hands) — holding something up.
目 (a container/tray) — held between the two hands, the image behind 具's meaning 'tool, utensil.'

example.hanzi: 锤子是一种常见的工具。
example.pinyin: Chuízi shì yì zhǒng chángjiàn de gōngjù.
example.english: A hammer is a common tool.
example.fact: 工具 reaches well past physical hammers and wrenches to cover any "instrument" or "means" for getting something done — 学习工具 ("learning tools"), 工具书 ("reference book," literally "tool book") — extending 工 ("work, labor") into anything that helps get work done.

components.note: 冎 pictures a joint of bone.
⺼ (flesh) sits below, together giving 骨 its meaning 'bone.'
大 (big) — in 头's simplified form, this element is linked to the idea of 'high' or topmost, since the head sits at the top of the body.

example.hanzi: 小狗正在啃一根骨头。
example.pinyin: Xiǎo gǒu zhèngzài kěn yì gēn gǔtou.
example.english: The puppy is gnawing on a bone.
example.fact: Beyond its literal anatomical sense, 骨头 extends metaphorically to a person's inner character — 硬骨头 ("hard bone") describes someone tough and unyielding, echoing how English also reaches for "spine" and "backbone" as stand-ins for moral fortitude.

components.note: 关 — a person's arms shown in a waving or embracing gesture, bidding farewell
辶 (to walk) — the person walking away who is being seen off
纟 (thread/silk) — 给 originally related to supplying thread or material, later broadening to mean 'to give.'
合 (hé) gives a hint of the sound — 给 is pronounced gěi, a connection that has shifted over time.

example.hanzi: 我把这本书送给你。
example.pinyin: Wǒ bǎ zhè běn shū sònggěi nǐ.
example.english: I'm giving you this book as a present.
example.fact: 送给 pairs two overlapping "giving" verbs back to back — 送 ("to give a gift, to see someone off") and 给 ("to give, for") — a common Mandarin strategy for pinning down exactly which sense of an ambiguous single-syllable verb is meant, here ruling out 送's other sense of "to escort, see off."

components.note: 酉 (wine jar) — 醒 originally described sobering up from drink, extending to 'to wake up.'
星 (xīng) gives a sound close to xǐng, sharing the same syllable body and differing mainly in tone.
Originally depicted a wheat plant; this agricultural picture was borrowed early on to represent the unrelated verb 'to come.'

example.hanzi: 他半夜醒来,再也睡不着了。
example.pinyin: Tā bànyè xǐnglái, zài yě shuì bu zháo le.
example.english: He woke up in the middle of the night and couldn't fall back asleep.
example.fact: 醒 (酉 "wine jar" + phonetic 星) originally described sobering up after drinking — 醒来, adding the directional complement 来 ("to come," marking a change occurring toward the present), extends that same "clearing of the mind" from intoxication to ordinary sleep.

components.note: 长 (simplified from 長) depicts an elderly figure with long flowing hair and a cane — length and seniority are linked in the original picture.

example.hanzi: 新市长上任后推出了不少新政策。
example.pinyin: Xīn shìzhǎng shàngrèn hòu tuīchū le bù shǎo xīn zhèngcè.
example.english: After taking office, the new mayor introduced quite a few new policies.
example.fact: 市长 literally means "city chief" — 市 ("city") plus 长, here read zhǎng ("head, chief") rather than its other reading cháng ("long") — the same zhǎng "head of" pattern recurs across titles like 校长 ("school principal") and 队长 ("team captain").

components.note: 田 (field) — represents farmland.
力 (strength/effort) — someone strong enough to work the fields gave 男 its meaning 'male, man.'
屮 (a young shoot) growing up out of 土 (earth/soil) — a picture of new life emerging from the ground.

example.hanzi: 班里的男生比女生多。
example.pinyin: Bān lǐ de nánshēng bǐ nǚshēng duō.
example.english: There are more boys than girls in the class.
example.fact: 男生 and its counterpart 女生 began as school vocabulary (生, "student," as in 学生) for "male/female student," but everyday spoken Mandarin has broadened both well past the classroom to mean simply "guy" and "girl" for young people in general.
